rows.label: Children's average blood lead in low- and middle-income countries (µg/dL)

source.title: Ericson B, Hu H, Nash E, Ferraro G, Sinitsky J, Taylor MP (2021), Blood lead levels in low-income and middle-income countries: a systematic review, The Lancet Planetary Health 5(3): e145-e153
source.quote: 632 million children (95% CI 394 million–780 million; 48·5%) were estimated to have a blood lead level exceeding the US Centers for Disease Control's reference value of 5 μg/dL.
source.note: With about half of the 1.30 billion children modelled above 5 µg/dL, the middle child is near 5 µg/dL; the pooled country means run from 1.66 µg/dL (Ethiopia) to 9.30 µg/dL (Palestine). The range takes in that spread across the countries a programme works in.

rows.explainer: The blood lead of a typical child in low- and middle-income countries: about 5 µg/dL, since about half the children Ericson et al. could model are above the 5 µg/dL reference value (3 to 8 across countries). Read by every model of ours that values lead exposure averted in these countries.

rows.label: IQ points lost per µg/dL of children's blood lead, at the levels of low- and middle-income countries

source.title: Lanphear BP et al. (2005), Low-level environmental lead exposure and children's intellectual function: an international pooled analysis, Environmental Health Perspectives 113(7): 894-899 (abstract, Europe PMC)
source.quote: The estimated IQ point decrements associated with an increase in blood lead from 2.4 to 10 microg/dL, 10 to 20 microg/dL, and 20 to 30 microg/dL were 3.9 (95% CI, 2.4-5.3), 1.9 (95% CI, 1.2-2.6), and 1.1 (95% CI, 0.7-1.5), respectively.
source.note: 3.9 points over 7.6 µg/dL is 0.51 a µg/dL between 2.4 and 10 µg/dL, the range children in these countries are in. Low end: GiveWell's Pure Earth BOTEC uses 0.15 (0.2 × 75%) per µg/dL throughout childhood; high end: the pooled analysis finds a steeper loss for children whose blood lead never exceeded 7.5 µg/dL.

rows.explainer: How many IQ points a child loses per µg/dL of blood lead at today's levels in low- and middle-income countries: 0.5 from the seven-cohort pooled analysis (3.9 points from 2.4 to 10 µg/dL), from 0.15 (GiveWell's Pure Earth sheet) to 0.8 (the steeper loss below 7.5 µg/dL). Read by every model that turns blood lead into IQ points: our own builds and, changed for consistency, the imports (GiveWell's Pure Earth BOTEC, Ambitious Impact's LaBri and Lead Research for Action reports, LEEP's own Malawi analysis), whose own slopes stay in their evaluator views.

rows.label: Share of children's blood lead that comes from lead paint, in low- and middle-income countries still selling it

source.title: Lead Exposure Elimination Project (2021), LEEP cost-effectiveness analysis - Malawi
source.page: p. 4, 'The proportion of lead exposure which is due to lead paint'
source.quote: We could not find evidence for the proportion of lead exposure that is due to paint in low and middle income countries, and therefore discount the 70% US estimate substantially to an estimate of 20% in Malawi.
source.note: LEEP calls it a major area of uncertainty. Other sources in these countries: informal battery recycling, spices, cookware, cosmetics, mining, old petrol lead in soil.

rows.explainer: No study measures how much of children's blood lead in these countries comes from paint. In the US, after leaded petrol, paint was about 70%; in low- and middle-income countries battery recycling, spices, cookware and cosmetics add much, and many rural homes are unpainted. Our judgment, 15% (4% to 40%), a little below LEEP's 20% for Malawi because it averages over countries where fewer homes are painted.

rows.label: Deaths attributed to lead exposure worldwide, 2023

source.title: WHO, Lead poisoning and health, fact sheet (10 June 2026), citing IHME's Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
source.quote: more than 3.5 million deaths globally were attributed to lead exposure in 2023, primarily due to cardiovascular effects

rows.explainer: Lead's deaths from all sources, mostly adults' heart disease from a lifetime's exposure. Read by every model of ours that values adults' lead deaths averted.

source.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, births per year (Our World in Data grapher)
source.note: UN DESA, World Population Prospects 2024, estimates variant, via Our World in Data's 'Number of births per year'.

rows.label: Years from a child's lead exposure to working age
rows.explainer: Lead harms the brain most before about age six (exposure centred near age three); earnings start at about 20. Our judgment, 17 years (14 to 20). Read by every model of ours that values children's lead exposure averted as later earnings.
